opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea here comes out of thinking about AI control: how do you get useful work out of models that might be scheming against you, without having to assume they're aligned?

One of the scariest threat models is the long-horizon one. The AI isn't trying to do something egregious in a single action, because that's the kind of thing a monitor might catch. Instead it pursues a plan spread over many steps: slowly accumulating knowledge about your security setup, inserting small, individually innocuous-looking pieces of code that only become dangerous in combination, or coordinating its future behavior by building up context over a long task. Many of the worst attacks we worry about, like exfiltrating weights or setting up a rogue internal deployment, plausibly need that kind of sustained, coherent effort.

Forced factored cognition is about denying the model that coherence. Instead of letting one instance of the model hold a huge context, work on a task for days, and keep a running picture of everything it's done, you break the work into small subtasks. Each is handled by a separate instance that sees only what it needs. One instance writes a plan, a different instance implements one piece of it, another reviews, and none of them has the full picture.

That makes attacks harder in a few ways.

First, it's much harder for the model to collude with itself across time. If the instance writing step seven doesn't know what happened in steps one through six, it can't build on a backdoor it planted earlier unless it can somehow recognize it, and recognizing it is itself a detectable signal.

Second, it limits situational awareness. A lot of what makes an attack succeed is knowing things like "the monitor isn't looking at this directory" or "this is a real deployment, not a test." If each instance has a narrow, curated context, it has much less information to make those judgments, so it's more likely to attack at the wrong moment and get caught, or not attack at all.

Third, it gives you natural chokepoints. The interfaces between subtasks are small, legible objects you can monitor, paraphrase, or sanitize. If one instance is trying to smuggle a message to a later instance, maybe through steganography in its outputs, you can rewrite those outputs with a trusted weaker model and break the channel.

Obviously it has costs. Factoring work is a performance hit, sometimes a big one, because a lot of real work benefits from one agent holding everything in its head. And there's a question about whether the decomposition itself leaks enough structure for a clever model to reconstruct what's going on. So I don't think of it as a silver bullet. But a big theme in control is that you don't need any single measure to be perfect. You need to make the attacker's job hard enough, and the chance of getting caught high enough, that across a whole deployment the expected outcome is that you catch them before they succeed. Breaking up long-horizon coherence is a pretty natural lever for that, because so many of the most dangerous attacks fundamentally depend on it.

r001.rationale: The response says subtask interfaces can be monitored, paraphrased, or sanitized, and that rewriting outputs can break steganographic messages to later instances.

r002.rationale: It explains that giving each instance a narrow, curated context limits situational awareness and makes sustained, long-horizon attacks harder.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea here is that a lot of the scariest things an AI could do, if it was trying to undermine you, are things that take a long time and involve many steps. Like, if you want to exfiltrate your own weights, or insert a backdoor into some piece of infrastructure, or slowly tamper with the training process for a successor model, that's not usually something you do in one action. It's a project. You need to remember what you did last week, you need to coordinate across lots of different contexts, you need to keep track of which parts of the plan are already in place.

And the thing about forced factored cognition is that you break the AI's work up into a bunch of pieces where each piece is being done by a fresh instance that doesn't have the context of the others. So you take a big task, you decompose it into subtasks, each subtask gets handed to a model that only sees that subtask and whatever information you've explicitly decided to pass along. And then crucially, the model doesn't get to carry secret state between those pieces. It can't just sort of privately remember, "Oh, right, I'm in the middle of the backdoor plan, step three is next."

So from the AI's perspective, if it wants to pull off some long-horizon attack, it has to somehow coordinate with copies of itself that it can't directly talk to. All the communication has to go through channels that you, the human overseer, can see. Which means it either has to put the plan into the visible outputs, which you can read and which you might catch, or it has to do something more like steganography, hiding messages in text that look innocuous. And steganography is hard, especially when you're also paraphrasing stuff between steps or having a weaker trusted model rewrite the intermediate outputs.

I want to be clear that this isn't magic. There are versions of attacks that are kind of robust to this. Like, if there's an obvious Schelling point, if every instance of the model independently thinks, "If I were trying to sabotage this, the obvious thing to do would be X," then they don't need to communicate, they can just all do X. So factoring doesn't help against attacks where coordination is cheap. But it does seem to make a big class of attacks a lot harder, the ones where the model needs to be stateful and patient and build something up over time. You're basically taking away its memory, and a lot of the really dangerous stuff requires memory.

The cost, of course, is that this probably makes the AI less capable at the task you actually wanted it to do. There's a real tradeoff there. Some tasks genuinely need a lot of context, and forcing them into little isolated pieces makes the work worse. So the way I think about it is, this is one tool in the toolbox, and you'd want to apply it more aggressively on the tasks where the downside of a successful attack is really bad, and less aggressively where you need the capability and the stakes are lower.

r001.rationale: The response says coordination must pass through overseer-visible outputs and explains that hiding messages in those outputs is difficult, especially when intermediate outputs are paraphrased or rewritten.

r002.rationale: The response says factoring takes away the AI’s memory and makes stateful, patient attacks that build over time a lot harder.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is to make it harder for an AI to carry out a plan that requires a lot of coherent thinking over time. Instead of having one agent that thinks for a long time, remembers everything, and takes a whole sequence of actions, you split the work into smaller tasks, with different instances doing different pieces and relatively restricted communication between them.

Suppose an AI notices an opportunity to subvert the system. It might need to investigate that opportunity, arrange some prerequisites, and then exploit it later. If its context gets reset between those steps, it has a problem: how does it get the next instance to continue the attack? It has to transmit enough information through some channel that we permit. And that gives us a place to monitor, or to restrict what gets passed along.

The important thing is that this has to be enforced by the setup. Asking an agent to delegate doesn't help much if it can simply keep a private record of its plan and coordinate everything itself.

I wouldn't expect this to rule out attacks. An attack might fit inside one task, or the instances might find ways to coordinate through apparently innocuous outputs. And there's a cost: some useful work also requires maintaining a lot of context. But potentially you can arrange things so that legitimate tasks decompose relatively well, while a long, covert attack is much harder to sustain across those boundaries.

r001.rationale: It says instances must pass information through permitted channels that can be monitored or restricted, making it harder to carry attack plans forward covertly.

r002.rationale: It explains that resetting context between tasks makes it harder to sustain an attack requiring coherent planning over time.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to make it harder for an AI to carry out a plan that requires a lot of coherent thinking over time. Instead of having one model work on a task for hours, remembering everything it’s done and developing its strategy, you split the work into small pieces. Each instance gets a limited amount of context, does a relatively short task, and passes its output back.

Suppose an AI wants to insert a subtle vulnerability into some code and then exploit it much later. It might need to understand the broader situation, choose a vulnerability, make sure it survives review, and arrange for some future action. If those steps are handled by separate instances that don’t share a private memory, that becomes more difficult. The plan has to travel through the messages between them, which gives us an opportunity to notice it.

There’s an important caveat, though: separate instances might coordinate without explicitly communicating the whole plan. They might all independently infer what strategy to follow, or hide information in outputs that look innocuous. So I wouldn’t claim that factoring the cognition makes attacks impossible. The hope is that it removes an easy way of sustaining a complicated attack, and forces more of the coordination through channels we can monitor.

r001.rationale: The response says messages between instances can be monitored, but it does not propose constraining progress reports to prevent covertly conveying information. It instead acknowledges that information could be hidden in innocuous-looking outputs.

r002.rationale: The response says each instance would have limited context and argues this would make sustaining a complicated attack over time more difficult.
